$comment: Architecture rules for the file-level dependency graph. Rules are data: each one states which files may depend on which, and what to do about the rest. scan.js evaluates them and emits violations.

layers.$comment: Each file maps to exactly one layer by path prefix, first match wins.

rules.description: lib/ holds host-agnostic shared facilities. It must not depend on any application layer; if a lib module needs core state, the state belongs in core and reaches lib through arguments, not imports.
Business logic must not depend on any client. The UI only renders what core emits.

core reaches tools only through the directory-scanning registry (slot loading). Any other core file depending on a tool is a hard-wired dependency that breaks the slot contract. Shared facilities belong in lib/.
rules.allowNote: core/tools/registry.js scans tools/*/registry.json and loads each entry; this is the declared slot loader, not a static dependency.

rules.description: The renderer must reach core through the transport (HTTP/IPC) and the preload bridge, never by requiring core modules directly.
The launcher coordinates (selects UI, starts transport); it must not depend on tools or individual UI modules except through the UIS registry.
Provider adapters are leaves: they shape provider-specific requests and must not pull in core, tools or UI.
Tools are replaceable slot implementations. They depend on lib/ for shared facilities and never on core internals. This rule is unconditional: no file exemptions are allowed.
Tools run in core's process and report results through the tool result contract; they never reach a client.

accounts/ holds the mechanics shared by both account slots: credential lifecycle, error taxonomy, outbound pacing and instance discovery. It is a leaf like lib/: it must not depend on core, tools, providers, clients, or on either slot it serves.

A channel is one authenticated external account binding. It reaches core only through the transport RPC surface (POST /api/call, fn=chat.send), never by importing core modules, and it must not depend on tools, providers or any client. Keeping this true is what allows a channel to run on another machine against a remote core.

A proxy acts as a person using that person's grant. It reaches core only through the transport RPC surface, never by importing core modules, and it must not depend on tools, providers, clients, or on channels. A proxy is invoked on demand; it has no inbound event stream.
Developer scripts are standalone tooling; depending on application code makes them break silently when app layers move.

cycles.$comment: Dependency cycles are not automatically wrong (store/compaction, context/compaction-runner legitimately interlock), so they are reported for review rather than failed.
